# The Portability Problem with PHP Short Tags

The official PHP documentation explicitly categorizes short tags (`<? ?>`) and ASP-style tags (`<% %>` ) as "generally not recommended" despite their convenience. While typing `<?=` is undeniably faster than `<?php echo`, the trade-off lies in portability rather than syntax correctness. The core issue is that these alternatives are controlled by server configuration, specifically the `short_open_tag` directive in `php.ini`.

When you enable short tags locally on a development machine but deploy to a production environment where they are disabled, your application breaks immediately. A file containing `<?=` will result in a parse error because the PHP interpreter ignores the closing tag entirely, treating the rest of the line as plain text or causing a syntax failure depending on the surrounding context. This fragmentation forces developers to maintain duplicate codebases: one version for local development and another for production, simply to accommodate different server configurations.

### The Configuration Dependency

The primary technical risk is the reliance on a global setting that can easily be misconfigured or changed without immediate warning. If a hosting provider disables `short_open_tag` by defaultâa common practice to prevent conflicts with other tags like `<%` used in ASP.NET or JSP filesâyour legacy code will fail to parse.

Consider a scenario where you have mixed content:

```php
<?
    echo "Short tag content";
?>

<%
    echo "ASP style tag content";
?>

<?php
    echo "Standard PHP tag content";
?>
```

On a server with `short_open_tag=On`, all three blocks execute. On a standard LAMP stack or most modern cloud providers, only the `<?php` block runs. The first two become HTML text output to the browser, potentially exposing logic errors if the code inside them isn't escaped properly. This inconsistency is why modern frameworks and best practices universally default to `<?php`.

### Integration with Modern Frameworks

This portability concern extends directly into the realm of modern PHP development. If you are building a standard application or integrating with a framework like Laravel, short tags introduce significant friction. While Laravel itself does not enforce the use of long tags in its core syntax, it relies on strict standards for compatibility across different environments.

Using `<?` in a Laravel project creates a fragile dependency. If your local `php.ini` has short tags enabled but the server running Laravel does not, you will encounter obscure "Call to undefined function" errors or unexpected output buffering issues because the parser never enters PHP mode for that line.

For projects hosted on platforms like https://laravelcompany.com or similar managed hosting environments, adhering to standard long tags ensures that your application behaves identically regardless of the underlying web server configuration (Apache, Nginx, or built-in SAPI). The cost of typing four extra characters (`php `) is negligible compared to the debugging time required to fix a parse error caused by a missing configuration directive.

### Best Practices for Legacy Code

If you inherit a codebase full of short tags, simply replacing them with long tags is often the safest migration path. This can be done via a global find-and-replace operation in your editor or through automated tools like `sed`. However, caution is required when dealing with mixed scripts containing HTML templates.

In blade templates or other templating engines, ensuring that the opening tag matches the expected standard prevents rendering issues. Always verify the runtime behavior of your code by checking the error logs on a fresh server instance where `short_open_tag` is explicitly set to `Off`. If your code runs without errors in that strict environment, it will run reliably everywhere else.

The industry has moved away from short tags because they introduce an unnecessary point of failure. The slight gain in typing speed does not justify the risk of environment-specific breakage. Sticking to `<?php` ensures that your application's logic is treated as executable code by every PHP interpreter, regardless of how the server was configured.
